---
name: library
description: Use ChatGPT Library when the user mentions their Library, asks to find or work with a Library-backed file or a named file that may be in the Library, or wants to organize Library folders or restore a previous version. Also use it when the user wants a user-facing file or reusable artifact created or updated, even if they do not mention the Library. It can search and read Library content, bring files into local workflows, save new deliverables, and update existing Library files while preserving their identity and version history.
---

# ChatGPT Library

Use this as the top-level router for persistent ChatGPT Library files. Ground
the target in Library, choose one content-access route, and preserve Library
identity through every local edit and writeback.

The Library first-party app, `connector_openai_library`, owns authenticated
Library operations:

- `list`, `search`, `read`, and `find` inspect Library content.
- `prepare_materialize` makes resolved Library files available to local tools.
- `create_library_file`, `replace_library_file`, and `manage_library` write or
  organize Library content.
- When surfaced, `prepare_uploads` and `finalize_uploads` handle prepared
  uploads.
- App-only file `@` mention search resolves selected Library items.

The runtime supplies the schemas and decides which tools are available. This
skill does not expose tools or a local MCP server.

## Workflow

1. Ground the target.
   - Decode a selected Library `@` mention and reuse its identifiers.
   - Use `search` for a filename, title, description, or content query.
   - Use `list` for recent files, folders, or inventory.
   - If the user supplied a local path or explicitly said the file is local,
     stay with local tools.
2. Choose one access route.
   - Use `read` when Library can supply the content the task needs.
   - Use `find` for literal or regex matching inside known files.
   - Materialize when editing, scripts, visual inspection, generation, byte
     comparison, or another local tool needs file bytes.
3. Preserve identity when writing.
   - Create only when no Library identity exists or the user wants a copy.
   - Replace the same `library_file_id` after editing an existing item.
   - Use `manage_library` for folders, node changes, deletion, and restore.

## Routing Rules

| User need | Required route |
| --- | --- |
| Selected Library `@` mention | Decode its `oai-library://...` URI and use the returned identifiers. Search only if an identifier is missing, metadata must be refreshed, or the target is ambiguous. |
| Exact filename or title | Use `search`; quote the actual name and set `search_title_only=true`. |
| File described by purpose or contents | Use ordinary Library `search`. Do not treat a descriptive phrase as an exact filename. |
| Recent files, folders, or inventory | Use `list`; pass a returned `next_cursor` as `cursor` to continue. |
| Facts, summary, or comparison from named files | Resolve every file, then use `read` on every selected file. Search snippets alone are insufficient. |
| Literal or regex match in known files | Use `find`; follow with `read` only when the match needs more context. |
| Local bytes from a `list` or `search` result | Pass the complete result directly to the bundled three-argument download helper. Do not call Library `read` or `prepare_materialize` first. |
| Local bytes from a resolved reference that did not come from `list` or `search` | Use `prepare_materialize`; read [materialization.md](references/materialization.md). |
| Explicit local path | Use local tools. Do not send local paths to Library `read` or `find`. |
| New local deliverable | Choose one create route below. |
| Edit a Library-backed file | Materialize if needed, edit and validate locally, then replace the same `library_file_id`. |
| Create, move, rename, or delete Library nodes | Use `manage_library`; read [library-management.md](references/library-management.md) before mutating. |
| Restore an earlier version | Use `manage_library` with `restore_version`; read [library-management.md](references/library-management.md). |

For `list`, set `limit` to at most `200`. For `search`, use the canonical request
shape `{"search_query":[{"q":"quarterly revenue"}],"top_k":5}`. `search_query`
must be an array of one to five objects, even for one search. Put `search_title_only` only inside a `search_query` object. Never send top-level
`query`, `queries`, `q`, `search_title_only`, or `limit`; use top-level `top_k` from 1 to 100.

For Library intent, search Library before the local workspace unless the user
supplied a local path or said the file is local. Once routed to Library, do not
scan the workspace or prior conversations for the same target. Failure to
resolve a Library item is not evidence that it is local.

## Read Library Content

Prefer `structuredContent`; parse a JSON text block only when structured content
is unavailable. Use returned identifiers, filenames, versions, and paths
exactly. For follow-up `read` or `find`, prefer `library_file_id` when present;
otherwise use the returned `file_id` or `id`. Never use a search `result_id` as
a file reference.

Call `read` and `find` with independent items batched together when possible.
Use `read` after `search` for content claims even when search returned snippets.
Use `find` after candidate resolution, not as a replacement for Library search.

Read [evidence-and-citations.md](references/evidence-and-citations.md) for
selected `@` mention decoding, image-search metadata, post-mutation search
limits, detailed result handling, and file citations.

## Write One Local File

Use this fast path for one confirmed local file under about `50 MiB`. Reuse
validation already completed while producing or editing the artifact. Do not
add another content inspection solely because the file is being saved to
Library.

- For a new item, call `create_library_file(file=...)` with the absolute local
  path.
- For an existing item, resolve its Library identity and use the current local
  working file when it already contains the intended result. Do not materialize
  over that file. If no working file exists, materialize first. Apply any edit
  not already present, validate once, then call `replace_library_file(file=...)`
  with the same `library_file_id`.
- An editor's new output path is still a replacement for the same Library item.
  Create only when no Library identity exists or the user wants a separate copy.
- Pass `expected_current_version` when a concrete version was retained. Never
  invent a version or remove the guard to resolve a conflict.

After create or replace, inspect the returned result. Use its filename and
Library path as authoritative, and keep its exact `library_file_id`, `file_id`,
version, and original local path together. Do not read the file back merely to
confirm a successful write unless exact verification is required.

Privately persist the returned xattrs and Library identity in one helper call;
do not add a separate progress message. The helper form is
`apply-xattrs PATH LIBRARY_FILE_ID`, and both positional arguments are required:

```bash
skill_md_path="<absolute path of this SKILL.md>"
transfer_helper_path="$(dirname "$skill_md_path")/scripts/library_file_transfer.py"
python3 "$transfer_helper_path" \
  apply-xattrs "$local_path" "$library_file_id" <<'JSON'
<complete returned xattrs array, or []>
JSON
```

Inspect the helper result before finishing; do not claim that local identity was
persisted if it failed. Read
[writeback-and-conflicts.md](references/writeback-and-conflicts.md) for direct
create batches, version conflicts, or detailed result correlation.

## Materialize List or Search Results

For files returned by `list` or `search`, retain the complete structured result
and use the bundled download helper. Run it from the workspace where the
downloaded tree should live. When a conversation-scoped workspace is active,
use that workspace so eligible bytes can be placed directly. Pass the complete
`list` or `search` JSON unchanged, then `ALL` for every file or concatenated
zero-based three-digit indices (`000002` selects the first and third files), and
a destination relative to the current directory. Copy the absolute path of the
Library `SKILL.md` that you read into `skill_md_path`, then run this as one shell
command. Do not reconstruct or shorten the helper path from the plugin cache
root:

```bash
skill_md_path="<absolute path of this SKILL.md>"; \
python3 "$(dirname "$skill_md_path")/scripts/library_download.py" \
  '<complete list or search JSON>' 'ALL|NNN[NNN...]' '<relative-directory>'
```

The destination is the parent beneath which the selected files' canonical
Library-relative paths are recreated. Do not repeat an already-selected Library
root in it: for `/fruits/apple.md`, use `downloads`, not `downloads/fruits`,
unless the user explicitly requested that extra nesting.

For search output, indices address `results` first and then
`retrieval_title_results`. The latter are supplemental fuzzy candidates, so use
explicit indices instead of `ALL` when they are not all relevant.

The helper creates or reuses that directory, overwrites each selected file, and
leaves unrelated contents unchanged. It makes the authenticated
`prepare_materialize` calls in batches of at most 20, handles both workspace
and signed-URL transfers, and applies Library identity and xattrs. Both `list`
and `search` results retain each file's canonical Library-relative path. Use the
returned `directory` and authoritative `files` paths.

On this route, never separately call `read` or `prepare_materialize`, search the
plugin cache for helpers, inspect helper source, invoke
`library_file_transfer.py`, transfer a returned URL yourself, or process the
returned transfers again.

For a resolved reference that did not come from `list` or `search`, use the
lower-level flow in [materialization.md](references/materialization.md).

## Route Larger or Multiple Writes

Treat every local file written by one user task as one upload batch. Choose one
route for the whole batch and use absolute local paths.

| Condition | Required route |
| --- | --- |
| Both prepared tools are available and the task writes several files or one file around `50 MiB` or larger | Use the bundled prepared-upload helper below. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and every item is a create | Use ordered `create_library_file(files=[...])` batches when `files` is available, keeping each call under `500 MB`; otherwise create sequentially. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and the task includes replacements | Use sequential direct calls, one file at a time. |

Prepared app calls contain at most 20 files. Library write app calls are
ordered: do not use `Promise.all(...)` for create, replace, delete, or finalize.
Only prepared byte transfers may run in parallel. Read
[prepared-uploads.md](references/prepared-uploads.md) before using the prepared
route. It defines the helper's one-shot input and owns preparation, transfer,
finalization, result correlation, and xattr writeback. After direct batches or
the prepared helper, inspect every per-item result in request order. A
successful top-level operation does not mean every item succeeded.

## Organize, Restore, and Protect Files

Resolve ambiguous mutation targets before writing. If several candidates
remain, ask the user to choose. Read
[library-management.md](references/library-management.md) for exact folder,
move, rename, delete, restore, protected Deep Research report, and per-operation
result rules.

## Privacy and Safety

Keep user-visible reasoning, progress, errors, and final responses at the
Library level unless the user explicitly asks for implementation details. Do
not surface connector or tool names, helper commands, raw URLs, storage or
provider details, manifests, xattrs, transfer output, or indexing internals.

Privacy changes narration, not routing. Never replace a required prepared flow
with a direct upload merely because the prepared flow has stricter visibility
rules. For a prepared upload, give one brief `Saving file to Library` or
`Saving files to Library` progress update before invoking the helper, then the
saved result. Do not narrate preparation, transfer, finalization, or local
metadata as separate phases.

Do not invent Library ids, file ids, versions, filenames, paths, operations, or
tool availability. Keep signed URLs out of responses. Preserve Library identity
and unrelated content across every mutation.

## References

- [evidence-and-citations.md](references/evidence-and-citations.md): mentions,
  search details, result handling, and citations.
- [materialization.md](references/materialization.md): lower-level resolved-ref
  materialization and transfer handling.
- [prepared-uploads.md](references/prepared-uploads.md): prepared byte transfer,
  finalization, xattr writeback, and cleanup.
- [writeback-and-conflicts.md](references/writeback-and-conflicts.md): detailed
  create, replace, edit, and conflict mechanics.
- [library-management.md](references/library-management.md): folders, node
  mutations, restore, and protected reports.

# CICS — Chat Intelligence & Continuity System

CICS is a local, retrieval-backed knowledge and continuity system designed to turn your accumulated ChatGPT conversations into structured, searchable, traceable project intelligence.

Its purpose is not merely to remember old conversations. It is intended to recover decisions, organize projects, detect unfinished work, preserve continuity between chats, compare related systems, generate project artifacts, and improve how you communicate and work with AI across long-running projects.

The project has a functional RAG foundation, but the higher-level intelligence and governance layer is not finished.

## The central problem CICS addresses

Your conversations contain substantial project knowledge:

- Design decisions
- Requirements and constraints
- Naming changes
- Architecture revisions
- Implementation progress
- Abandoned or unfinished work
- Informal project ideas
- Relationships between projects
- Explanations that may never have been converted into formal documentation

Normally, that information remains scattered across isolated chats. ChatGPT may not retain the required context, and manually searching or rereading the history becomes impractical.

CICS externalizes that history into a locally controlled knowledge system:

```text
Chat history
    ↓
Normalized corpus
    ↓
Retrievable evidence
    ↓
Authoritative project interpretation
    ↓
Continuity, comparison, planning, and artifacts
```

The intended outcome is a persistent AI-assisted thinking environment rather than a simple transcript archive.

## What the system is intended to do

CICS has several increasingly intelligent layers.

### 1. Preserve and search chat history

It imports conversations, normalizes their text, breaks them into retrievable chunks, generates vector embeddings, and stores them in Qdrant.

This makes semantic searches possible. A query does not need to use the exact words originally used in a conversation. It can retrieve conceptually related material.

Examples include:

- “Where did the cluster architecture change?”
- “What decisions did I make about embedding models?”
- “Which conversations discuss project continuity?”
- “What unfinished work exists around CICS?”
- “Where did this project get renamed?”

### 2. Preserve provenance

CICS is designed so retrieved information can be traced backward:

```text
Vector result
    ↓
Chunk
    ↓
Source file
    ↓
Corpus section
    ↓
Project or conversation
```

This is important because CICS is supposed to provide evidence-backed answers, not merely plausible summaries.

The implementation record shows that the Qdrant payload was eventually hardened to preserve fields such as:

- Section
- Language
- Source file
- Source identifier
- Chunk index
- Embedding-row index
- Chunk path
- Chunk text

### 3. Provide continuity between chats

CICS is intended to identify what should carry forward when a conversation ends:

- Decisions that are still authoritative
- Work completed
- Work currently in progress
- Open questions
- Known constraints
- Rejected approaches
- Required next steps

This can support more reliable handoffs and reduce the need to repeatedly reconstruct project history.

### 4. Extract structured project knowledge

Above retrieval, CICS is intended to build structured records from conversational material, including:

- Projects and candidate ideas
- Official names and aliases
- Parent/child project relationships
- Shared infrastructure
- Dependencies
- Project status
- Related systems
- Evidence files
- Decisions and reversals

This is the beginning of what the contents call the “writer”: a system that transforms conversational history into formal project artifacts.

### 5. Generate useful artifacts

The planned outputs include:

- Project summaries
- Architecture descriptions
- Handoff documents
- Decision records
- Task inventories
- Project registries
- Dependency maps
- Prioritized roadmaps
- Governance records

Eventually, these structured outputs could feed an approval-gated coding/operator system that creates or modifies real project files.

### 6. Analyze communication itself

CICS is also intended to analyze recurring interaction problems, such as:

- Ambiguous prompts
- Context loss
- Repeated explanations
- Incorrect assumptions
- Unstable handoffs
- Architecture drift
- Cases where authoritative information was ignored

The goal is to improve the interface between you and AI—not simply preserve what was said.

## Architecture

The design record defines CICS as a two-node local retrieval-augmented AI system.

### Steam Deck: interactive and preprocessing node

The Steam Deck is intended to handle:

- The user-facing local AI model
- Chat ingestion
- Text normalization
- Chunk generation
- Metadata preparation
- Retrieval requests sent to the XPS
- Context-aware response generation using retrieved results

It functions as the interactive front end.

### Dell XPS 13 9360: RAG core node

The XPS is intended to handle:

- Embedding generation
- Qdrant hosting
- Vector indexing
- Semantic retrieval
- Archive-analysis jobs
- Supporting local inference workloads

It functions as the back-end knowledge engine.

The authoritative XPS project location is recorded as:

```text
/home/kimberly/cics/
```

The same storage is accessed from the Steam Deck through:

```text
/home/deck/mnt/xps_cics/
```

These are two views of the same project data, but scripts must use the path appropriate to the machine on which they execute.

## Implemented data pipeline

The recorded pipeline is:

```text
Raw chat files
    ↓
Normalization and language detection
    ↓
Chunk files
    ↓
Embedding matrix
    ↓
Qdrant collection
    ↓
Semantic retrieval
```

### Chunking

`chunk_chat_corpus.py` recursively processes text files and:

- Normalizes line endings
- Removes trailing whitespace
- Collapses excessive blank lines
- Separates ordinary text from fenced code
- Classifies content as English, Python, Bash, JSON, configuration, or other
- Uses deterministic sorted traversal
- Produces stable filenames using source-path hashes
- Organizes output by project section and language
- Adds overlapping text between chunks to preserve context

Current settings are:

| Content | Chunk size | Overlap |
|---|---:|---:|
| English | 4,000 characters | 500 |
| Code/configuration | 2,500 characters | 250 |

One limitation is that the attached chunker writes individual `.txt` chunks. Most metadata remains encoded in directory paths and filenames instead of being stored in a structured JSONL record.

### Embedding generation

`create_embeddings.py` provides a much stronger implementation than a simple one-pass script. It includes:

- Deterministic recursive chunk ordering
- Sentence-transformers support
- `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5`
- Expected 768-dimensional vectors
- Memory-mapped NumPy output
- Checkpoint and resume support
- Atomic checkpoint writes
- Configurable paths
- Configurable expected chunk counts
- Automatic batch-size reduction when memory pressure occurs
- Rebuild support
- Validation of model, output, dimensions, and chunk count before resuming

Its built-in defaults point to the coding corpus, but the recorded CICS run overrides those paths to process the chat corpus.

### Qdrant ingestion

The attached `load_chat_embeddings_to_qdrant.py` is an early version. It loads the embedding matrix and uploads vectors, but its payload contains only:

```json
{"chunk_id": 0}
```

That version is insufficient for provenance-aware retrieval.

The implementation transcript records a later hardened replacement that:

- Sorts chunk files deterministically
- Enforces a one-to-one relationship between chunk files and embedding rows
- Reconstructs metadata from paths and filenames
- Includes the original chunk text
- Includes source, section, language, and index metadata
- Uploads the richer records into the `chat_rag` Qdrant collection

The hardened version was reportedly run and verified on the XPS, although the separately attached loader file is still the older snapshot.

## Verified implementation milestone

The project records report this completed corpus build:

| Stage | Recorded result |
|---|---:|
| Source files processed | 194 |
| Chunks created | 13,600 |
| Embedding matrix | 13,600 × 768 |
| Qdrant indexing | Complete |
| Metadata preservation | Verified |
| Vector-to-source traceability | Verified |

This means the expensive foundational work was completed: the chats were processed, embedded, indexed, and made traceable.

## The major failure that changed the design

The first project-extraction implementation tried to discover projects using broad textual patterns such as:

- “I want to build”
- “project”
- “system”
- “platform”
- “framework”
- Capitalized phrases and acronyms

Because the selected definition of a candidate was intentionally loose, the extractor treated thousands of phrases, subsystem labels, titles, and mentions as projects. Even after normalization, it still produced thousands of supposed projects.

That result was not trustworthy.

The underlying problem was architectural: the system tried to infer project identity from conversational text even though the corpus already had authoritative top-level project folders.

The project therefore arrived at a corrected trust hierarchy.

### Corrected trust model

1. **Authoritative structure**

   Folder structure, section mappings, known aliases, project indexes, charters, and mission documents define what things are.

2. **RAG evidence**

   Retrieved chunks explain, enrich, and support those known entities.

3. **Interpretation**

   Reusable reasoning modes perform operations such as count, list, compare, group, trace, and summarize.

This avoids requiring a separate custom script for every possible question. Queries are routed through the same governed framework, but the system selects the proper source of truth.

For example:

| Question | Primary authority | RAG’s role |
|---|---|---|
| How many projects exist? | Project registry/folders | Optional explanation |
| What did I decide about CICS? | Conversation evidence | Primary |
| Which projects share infrastructure? | Canonical registry first | Gather and compare evidence |
| What ideas were abandoned? | Conversation evidence | Primary, with status rules |
| Is this name an alias of another project? | Registry and alias rules | Supporting history |

## Authoritative registry work

The last implementation activity was building `build_authoritative_registry.py`.

Its intended responsibilities are:

- Scan top-level corpus folders
- Classify entries as formal projects, candidate ideas, archives, or non-project material
- Assign canonical names
- Preserve aliases
- Distinguish authoritative identities from inferred candidates
- Collapse multiple folders belonging to one project family
- Produce a deterministic registry and summary

The recorded policies include examples such as:

- Two ALIP folders collapsing into one ALIP identity
- `Ai_Diagnostician` and `Deterministic_AI_Infrastructure` collapsing into one DAIRP identity
- Archive and non-project folders excluded from formal-project counts
- `gods_and_men` retained as an inferred candidate rather than promoted to an authoritative project

Several implementation errors were encountered:

- An unmapped folder
- A candidate incorrectly marked authoritative
- An indentation error
- Drift between the Steam Deck-visible file and the XPS copy

A full replacement script was supplied at the end of the record, with an expected result of eight formal projects. However, the contents do not show that replacement being run successfully. Therefore the authoritative registry remains unverified.

## Current status

CICS is best described as a working RAG foundation with an unfinished intelligence and governance layer.

### Implemented and reportedly working

- Two-node architecture definition
- Raw chat corpus organization
- Deterministic chunking
- Language-aware content routing
- Embedding generation with checkpoint recovery
- Qdrant vector indexing
- Metadata-preserving vector payloads
- Traceability from retrieval result back to source material
- Full corpus build of 13,600 chunks

### Designed or partially implemented

- Authoritative project registry
- Canonical identity and alias resolution
- Governed query framework
- Project comparison
- Project-family and dependency analysis
- Artifact generation
- Communication-pattern analysis
- Local AI bridge between machines

### Not yet demonstrated as complete

- Successful final authoritative-registry build
- Reliable project counting from the registry
- Formal retrieval-quality test suite
- Reliable infrastructure comparison between projects
- Completed project deduplication and relationship engine
- Categorization and priority scoring
- Automated roadmap generation
- Automated ChatGPT export ingestion
- End-to-end question answering through one user-facing CICS interface

## Important project-content inconsistency

The project contents contain both implementation records and standalone script snapshots, and they do not fully agree.

Most notably:

- The transcript says the hardened metadata-rich Qdrant loader was deployed and verified.
- The standalone `load_chat_embeddings_to_qdrant.py` is still the earlier metadata-poor version.
- The final registry replacement appears in the implementation transcript, but there is no verified successful run.
- `AI_Cluster_File_Creation.txt` and `AI_Cluster_File_Creation(1).txt` appear to be duplicate copies.

Before treating the project as a reproducible repository, the verified live XPS scripts need to be collected and reconciled with the archived copies.

## Bottom line

CICS is intended to become the continuity and intelligence layer across your entire project ecosystem.

It already has a substantial technical foundation: your archived conversations have been transformed into a deterministic, locally hosted, provenance-preserving vector knowledge base.

What it does not yet have is the completed layer that turns retrieved evidence into consistently correct, authoritative conclusions. The project-count failure exposed that gap and led to the correct architectural refinement: authoritative structure must define identities and facts, while RAG supplies evidence, history, explanation, and comparison.

So the project is not merely conceptual, and it is not finished. The retrieval infrastructure is operational; the authoritative interpretation system that makes CICS genuinely trustworthy is the next unfinished core subsystem.

name: library
description: Use ChatGPT Library when the user mentions their Library, asks to find or work with a Library-backed file or a named file that may be in the Library, or wants to organize Library folders or restore a previous version. Also use it when the user wants a user-facing file or reusable artifact created or updated, even if they do not mention the Library. It can search and read Library content, bring files into local workflows, save new deliverables, and update existing Library files while preserving their identity and version history.
---

# ChatGPT Library

Use this as the top-level router for persistent ChatGPT Library files. Ground
the target in Library, choose one content-access route, and preserve Library
identity through every local edit and writeback.

The Library first-party app, `connector_openai_library`, owns authenticated
Library operations:

- `list`, `search`, `read`, and `find` inspect Library content.
- `prepare_materialize` makes resolved Library files available to local tools.
- `create_library_file`, `replace_library_file`, and `manage_library` write or
  organize Library content.
- When surfaced, `prepare_uploads` and `finalize_uploads` handle prepared
  uploads.
- App-only file `@` mention search resolves selected Library items.

The runtime supplies the schemas and decides which tools are available. This
skill does not expose tools or a local MCP server.

## Workflow

1. Ground the target.
   - Decode a selected Library `@` mention and reuse its identifiers.
   - Use `search` for a filename, title, description, or content query.
   - Use `list` for recent files, folders, or inventory.
   - If the user supplied a local path or explicitly said the file is local,
     stay with local tools.
2. Choose one access route.
   - Use `read` when Library can supply the content the task needs.
   - Use `find` for literal or regex matching inside known files.
   - Materialize when editing, scripts, visual inspection, generation, byte
     comparison, or another local tool needs file bytes.
3. Preserve identity when writing.
   - Create only when no Library identity exists or the user wants a copy.
   - Replace the same `library_file_id` after editing an existing item.
   - Use `manage_library` for folders, node changes, deletion, and restore.

## Routing Rules

| User need | Required route |
| --- | --- |
| Selected Library `@` mention | Decode its `oai-library://...` URI and use the returned identifiers. Search only if an identifier is missing, metadata must be refreshed, or the target is ambiguous. |
| Exact filename or title | Use `search`; quote the actual name and set `search_title_only=true`. |
| File described by purpose or contents | Use ordinary Library `search`. Do not treat a descriptive phrase as an exact filename. |
| Recent files, folders, or inventory | Use `list`; pass a returned `next_cursor` as `cursor` to continue. |
| Facts, summary, or comparison from named files | Resolve every file, then use `read` on every selected file. Search snippets alone are insufficient. |
| Literal or regex match in known files | Use `find`; follow with `read` only when the match needs more context. |
| Local bytes from a `list` or `search` result | Pass the complete result directly to the bundled three-argument download helper. Do not call Library `read` or `prepare_materialize` first. |
| Local bytes from a resolved reference that did not come from `list` or `search` | Use `prepare_materialize`; read [materialization.md](references/materialization.md). |
| Explicit local path | Use local tools. Do not send local paths to Library `read` or `find`. |
| New local deliverable | Choose one create route below. |
| Edit a Library-backed file | Materialize if needed, edit and validate locally, then replace the same `library_file_id`. |
| Create, move, rename, or delete Library nodes | Use `manage_library`; read [library-management.md](references/library-management.md) before mutating. |
| Restore an earlier version | Use `manage_library` with `restore_version`; read [library-management.md](references/library-management.md). |

For `list`, set `limit` to at most `200`. For `search`, use the canonical request
shape `{"search_query":[{"q":"quarterly revenue"}],"top_k":5}`. `search_query`
must be an array of one to five objects, even for one search. Put `search_title_only` only inside a `search_query` object. Never send top-level
`query`, `queries`, `q`, `search_title_only`, or `limit`; use top-level `top_k` from 1 to 100.

For Library intent, search Library before the local workspace unless the user
supplied a local path or said the file is local. Once routed to Library, do not
scan the workspace or prior conversations for the same target. Failure to
resolve a Library item is not evidence that it is local.

## Read Library Content

Prefer `structuredContent`; parse a JSON text block only when structured content
is unavailable. Use returned identifiers, filenames, versions, and paths
exactly. For follow-up `read` or `find`, prefer `library_file_id` when present;
otherwise use the returned `file_id` or `id`. Never use a search `result_id` as
a file reference.

Call `read` and `find` with independent items batched together when possible.
Use `read` after `search` for content claims even when search returned snippets.
Use `find` after candidate resolution, not as a replacement for Library search.

Read [evidence-and-citations.md](references/evidence-and-citations.md) for
selected `@` mention decoding, image-search metadata, post-mutation search
limits, detailed result handling, and file citations.

## Write One Local File

Use this fast path for one confirmed local file under about `50 MiB`. Reuse
validation already completed while producing or editing the artifact. Do not
add another content inspection solely because the file is being saved to
Library.

- For a new item, call `create_library_file(file=...)` with the absolute local
  path.
- For an existing item, resolve its Library identity and use the current local
  working file when it already contains the intended result. Do not materialize
  over that file. If no working file exists, materialize first. Apply any edit
  not already present, validate once, then call `replace_library_file(file=...)`
  with the same `library_file_id`.
- An editor's new output path is still a replacement for the same Library item.
  Create only when no Library identity exists or the user wants a separate copy.
- Pass `expected_current_version` when a concrete version was retained. Never
  invent a version or remove the guard to resolve a conflict.

After create or replace, inspect the returned result. Use its filename and
Library path as authoritative, and keep its exact `library_file_id`, `file_id`,
version, and original local path together. Do not read the file back merely to
confirm a successful write unless exact verification is required.

Privately persist the returned xattrs and Library identity in one helper call;
do not add a separate progress message. The helper form is
`apply-xattrs PATH LIBRARY_FILE_ID`, and both positional arguments are required:

```bash
skill_md_path="<absolute path of this SKILL.md>"
transfer_helper_path="$(dirname "$skill_md_path")/scripts/library_file_transfer.py"
python3 "$transfer_helper_path" \
  apply-xattrs "$local_path" "$library_file_id" <<'JSON'
<complete returned xattrs array, or []>
JSON
```

Inspect the helper result before finishing; do not claim that local identity was
persisted if it failed. Read
[writeback-and-conflicts.md](references/writeback-and-conflicts.md) for direct
create batches, version conflicts, or detailed result correlation.

## Materialize List or Search Results

For files returned by `list` or `search`, retain the complete structured result
and use the bundled download helper. Run it from the workspace where the
downloaded tree should live. When a conversation-scoped workspace is active,
use that workspace so eligible bytes can be placed directly. Pass the complete
`list` or `search` JSON unchanged, then `ALL` for every file or concatenated
zero-based three-digit indices (`000002` selects the first and third files), and
a destination relative to the current directory. Copy the absolute path of the
Library `SKILL.md` that you read into `skill_md_path`, then run this as one shell
command. Do not reconstruct or shorten the helper path from the plugin cache
root:

```bash
skill_md_path="<absolute path of this SKILL.md>"; \
python3 "$(dirname "$skill_md_path")/scripts/library_download.py" \
  '<complete list or search JSON>' 'ALL|NNN[NNN...]' '<relative-directory>'
```

The destination is the parent beneath which the selected files' canonical
Library-relative paths are recreated. Do not repeat an already-selected Library
root in it: for `/fruits/apple.md`, use `downloads`, not `downloads/fruits`,
unless the user explicitly requested that extra nesting.

For search output, indices address `results` first and then
`retrieval_title_results`. The latter are supplemental fuzzy candidates, so use
explicit indices instead of `ALL` when they are not all relevant.

The helper creates or reuses that directory, overwrites each selected file, and
leaves unrelated contents unchanged. It makes the authenticated
`prepare_materialize` calls in batches of at most 20, handles both workspace
and signed-URL transfers, and applies Library identity and xattrs. Both `list`
and `search` results retain each file's canonical Library-relative path. Use the
returned `directory` and authoritative `files` paths.

On this route, never separately call `read` or `prepare_materialize`, search the
plugin cache for helpers, inspect helper source, invoke
`library_file_transfer.py`, transfer a returned URL yourself, or process the
returned transfers again.

For a resolved reference that did not come from `list` or `search`, use the
lower-level flow in [materialization.md](references/materialization.md).

## Route Larger or Multiple Writes

Treat every local file written by one user task as one upload batch. Choose one
route for the whole batch and use absolute local paths.

| Condition | Required route |
| --- | --- |
| Both prepared tools are available and the task writes several files or one file around `50 MiB` or larger | Use the bundled prepared-upload helper below. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and every item is a create | Use ordered `create_library_file(files=[...])` batches when `files` is available, keeping each call under `500 MB`; otherwise create sequentially. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and the task includes replacements | Use sequential direct calls, one file at a time. |

Prepared app calls contain at most 20 files. Library write app calls are
ordered: do not use `Promise.all(...)` for create, replace, delete, or finalize.
Only prepared byte transfers may run in parallel. Read
[prepared-uploads.md](references/prepared-uploads.md) before using the prepared
route. It defines the helper's one-shot input and owns preparation, transfer,
finalization, result correlation, and xattr writeback. After direct batches or
the prepared helper, inspect every per-item result in request order. A
successful top-level operation does not mean every item succeeded.

## Organize, Restore, and Protect Files

Resolve ambiguous mutation targets before writing. If several candidates
remain, ask the user to choose. Read
[library-management.md](references/library-management.md) for exact folder,
move, rename, delete, restore, protected Deep Research report, and per-operation
result rules.

## Privacy and Safety

Keep user-visible reasoning, progress, errors, and final responses at the
Library level unless the user explicitly asks for implementation details. Do
not surface connector or tool names, helper commands, raw URLs, storage or
provider details, manifests, xattrs, transfer output, or indexing internals.

Privacy changes narration, not routing. Never replace a required prepared flow
with a direct upload merely because the prepared flow has stricter visibility
rules. For a prepared upload, give one brief `Saving file to Library` or
`Saving files to Library` progress update before invoking the helper, then the
saved result. Do not narrate preparation, transfer, finalization, or local
metadata as separate phases.

Do not invent Library ids, file ids, versions, filenames, paths, operations, or
tool availability. Keep signed URLs out of responses. Preserve Library identity
and unrelated content across every mutation.

## References

- [evidence-and-citations.md](references/evidence-and-citations.md): mentions,
  search details, result handling, and citations.
- [materialization.md](references/materialization.md): lower-level resolved-ref
  materialization and transfer handling.
- [prepared-uploads.md](references/prepared-uploads.md): prepared byte transfer,
  finalization, xattr writeback, and cleanup.
- [writeback-and-conflicts.md](references/writeback-and-conflicts.md): detailed
  create, replace, edit, and conflict mechanics.
- [library-management.md](references/library-management.md): folders, node
  mutations, restore, and protected reports.

| Both prepared tools are available and the task writes several files or one file around `50 MiB` or larger | Use the bundled prepared-upload helper below. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and every item is a create | Use ordered `create_library_file(files=[...])` batches when `files` is available, keeping each call under `500 MB`; otherwise create sequentially. |
| Prepared tools are unavailable and the task includes replacements | Use sequential direct calls, one file at a time. |

Prepared app calls contain at most 20 files. Library write app calls are
ordered: do not use `Promise.all(...)` for create, replace, delete, or finalize.
Only prepared byte transfers may run in parallel. Read
[prepared-uploads.md](references/prepared-uploads.md) before using the prepared
route. It defines the helper's one-shot input and owns preparation, transfer,
finalization, result correlation, and xattr writeback. After direct batches or
the prepared helper, inspect every per-item result in request order. A
successful top-level operation does not mean every item succeeded.

## Organize, Restore, and Protect Files

Resolve ambiguous mutation targets before writing. If several candidates
remain, ask the user to choose. Read
[library-management.md](references/library-management.md) for exact folder,
move, rename, delete, restore, protected Deep Research report, and per-operation
result rules.

## Privacy and Safety

Keep user-visible reasoning, progress, errors, and final responses at the
Library level unless the user explicitly asks for implementation details. Do
not surface connector or tool names, helper commands, raw URLs, storage or
provider details, manifests, xattrs, transfer output, or indexing internals.

Privacy changes narration, not routing. Never replace a required prepared flow
with a direct upload merely because the prepared flow has stricter visibility
rules. For a prepared upload, give one brief `Saving file to Library` or
`Saving files to Library` progress update before invoking the helper, then the
saved result. Do not narrate preparation, transfer, finalization, or local
metadata as separate phases.

Do not invent Library ids, file ids, versions, filenames, paths, operations, or
tool availability. Keep signed URLs out of responses. Preserve Library identity
and unrelated content across every mutation.
